quiz.question: `const n = "5" as number;` — result?
options: Compile error: conversion may be a mistake
quiz.explanation: `as` refuses conversions between types that don't overlap (TS2352). It never converts anything anyway.

quiz.question: `const el = {} as { id: string }; el.id.length` — what happens?
options: It compiles, then crashes at runtime: `el.id` is `undefined`
quiz.explanation: The assertion lied, and nothing at runtime notices until the property is used.

quiz.question: `const c = { mode: "dark" } satisfies { mode: "dark" | "light" };` — what is `c.mode`'s type?
quiz.explanation: `satisfies` checks the shape but keeps the expression's own, narrower type.

quiz.question: `type P = { x: number }; const p: P = { x: 1, y: 2 };` — result?
options: Compile error: `y` is an excess property
quiz.explanation: A fresh literal with unknown keys is almost always a typo (TS2353).

quiz.question: `function len(x: { length: number }) { … }` — is `len("abc")` allowed?
options: Yes — a string has a numeric `length`
quiz.explanation: Structural typing: anything with the right members fits.

quiz.question: Can an instance of `class A { x = 1 }` be used where `class B { x = 1 }` is expected?
options: Yes — they have the same structure
quiz.explanation: Classes compare structurally, as long as neither has private or protected members.

quiz.question: What makes two structurally identical classes incompatible?
quiz.explanation: Private members are compared by where they were declared, which makes classes that have them nominal.

quiz.question: Is `(x: string) => void` assignable to `(x: string | number) => void`?
options: No — the target may call it with a number it can't handle
quiz.explanation: Parameters are contravariant: the substitute must accept at least everything the original accepts.

quiz.question: Is `(x: string | number) => void` assignable to `(x: string) => void`?
options: Yes — it accepts everything it will be given, and more
Only if it returns a value
quiz.explanation: Accepting a wider parameter type is always safe.

quiz.question: Why write `const ROUTES = { … } as const satisfies Record<string, string>`?
options: To keep a read-only, literal-typed object while still checking its shape
To convert it to a Map
quiz.explanation: `as const` freezes the literal types; `satisfies` validates them without widening.

quiz.question: What does `satisfies` do that a type annotation does not?
options: It validates the value against the type while keeping the value's own narrower inferred type
It validates the value at runtime
It widens the value to the given type
quiz.explanation: An annotation replaces the inferred type; `satisfies` only checks against it. That is how you keep literal key and tuple information while still enforcing a contract.

quiz.question: With `const routes = { home: "/" } satisfies Record<string, string>`, what is `keyof typeof routes`?
quiz.explanation: The inferred object type is preserved, so its keys are the literal union of what was actually written. With a plain `Record<string, string>` annotation it would have been `string`.

quiz.question: Does `satisfies` help validate JSON arriving from a network call?
options: No — it is erased at compile time and checks nothing at runtime
Yes, it throws when the shape does not match
Yes, but only in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Like every type-level construct it disappears before the code runs. Runtime data still needs a type predicate or a schema validator.

quiz.question: `const bad: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, label: "home" };` errors, but assigning the same object through a variable does not. Why?
options: The excess property check only applies to fresh object literals assigned directly
Variables are always typed as any
The variable version is also an error, just reported later
label is a reserved property name
quiz.explanation: TypeScript treats a directly-assigned literal as a place where extra keys are almost certainly typos, so it checks them. Once the object is widened into a variable, ordinary structural assignability applies.

quiz.question: Two unrelated aliases `type A = { id: number }` and `type B = { id: number }`. Is `const b: B = someA;` legal?
options: Yes — structural typing compares shapes, not declaration names
No — they are different named types
Only when both are interfaces rather than type aliases
quiz.explanation: Nothing links A and B by name, but they have identical members, so each is assignable to the other. This is the core difference from Java's nominal `implements`.

quiz.question: What makes a class NOT purely structural in TypeScript?
options: Having private or protected members, which only match members from the same declaration
quiz.explanation: Private and protected members are tied to their declaring class, so two classes with identical-looking private fields are not interchangeable — the one nominal corner of the type system.

flashcards.front: When is `x as unknown as T` needed?

flashcards.front: `: T` vs `as T` vs `satisfies T` on an object literal?

flashcards.front: Why use `satisfies` on a config table?

flashcards.front: What is structural typing?
flashcards.back: Compatibility by shape, not by name: any value with the required members fits, whatever it was declared as.

flashcards.front: A variable with extra properties is assigned to a narrower type. What happens to the extras at runtime?
flashcards.back: They stay. The type just stops mentioning them — `Object.keys` still lists them.

flashcards.front: Why are excess-property errors only reported for literals?

flashcards.front: Why is `Dog[]` assignable to `Animal[]` a hole in the type system?

flashcards.front: Contravariance in one sentence?
flashcards.back: A function that accepts `Animal` can stand in for one that accepts `Dog` — not the other way round.

flashcards.front: Why are methods declared with method syntax riskier than function-typed properties?
flashcards.back: Method parameters are checked bivariantly even under `strictFunctionTypes`, so an unsafe override compiles.

flashcards.front: TS1360 — cause?

flashcards.front: Why test membership with `Object.hasOwn(obj, k)` instead of `k in obj`?
flashcards.back: `in` also sees inherited properties — `"toString" in {}` is `true`.

quiz.question: What does a brand cost at runtime?
options: Nothing — the intersection is erased and the value stays a plain string
A hidden property on each value
quiz.explanation: That is the appeal over a wrapper class: nominal safety with zero runtime representation.

quiz.question: What does `readonly string[]` prevent?
options: Calling mutating methods and assigning to indices
quiz.explanation: It is a compile-time restriction on the array's own operations. `const` only stops rebinding the variable.

quiz.question: Does `Object.freeze` give you a deeply immutable object?
options: No — it is shallow; nested objects remain mutable
quiz.explanation: Freezing one level is the runtime counterpart to `Readonly<T>`, which is also shallow. Deep immutability needs a recursive helper.

quiz.question: `type UserId = string & { __brand: "UserId" }; const id: UserId = "u1";` — result?
options: Compile error: a plain string isn't a `UserId`
quiz.explanation: The brand is the point: only your constructor, with its one cast, can make a `UserId`.

quiz.question: Can a `UserId` be passed to a function expecting a plain `string`?
options: Yes — a brand is a subtype of `string`
Only if the function is generic
quiz.explanation: Branding restricts which values *become* a `UserId`, not where one can go.

quiz.question: `const a = Object.freeze([1, 2]); a.push(3);` — does it compile?
options: Yes, but it throws at runtime
Yes, and the push is silently ignored
quiz.explanation: The type of a frozen array has no mutators, so the compiler stops you before the runtime would.

quiz.question: `const o = Object.freeze({ inner: { n: 1 } }); o.inner.n = 2;` — what happens?
options: It compiles and works — `freeze` is shallow
quiz.explanation: Only `o`'s own properties are frozen; `inner` is an ordinary object.

quiz.question: With `x: Readonly<{ a: { b: number } }>`, is `x.a.b = 2` allowed?
quiz.explanation: `x.a` can't be reassigned, but the object it points to is still mutable.

quiz.question: What is structural sharing?
options: A new version of a data structure reusing the unchanged parts of the old one
Two variables pointing at one object
quiz.explanation: It makes immutable updates cheap: changing one field copies only the path to it.

quiz.question: How do you add `x` to an array without mutating it?
quiz.explanation: Spread builds a new array; `push` changes the original.

quiz.question: How do you remove the element at index `i` without mutating?
quiz.explanation: `splice` mutates; `delete` leaves a hole.

quiz.question: How do you update one field of an object immutably?
quiz.explanation: `Object.assign(obj, …)` writes into `obj`; spreading into a new literal doesn't.

quiz.question: What does a `unique symbol` brand give you over a string-literal brand?
options: It can't be forged by writing the property name by hand
quiz.explanation: Every `unique symbol` declaration is its own type, so no other code can produce a matching key.

quiz.question: Is `as const` deep?
options: Yes — nested object and array literals become readonly too
quiz.explanation: `as const` applies recursively to the whole literal expression (unlike `Readonly<T>`).

quiz.question: Why should the constructor function be the ONLY place that writes `as UserId`?
options: It concentrates the unchecked assertion in one validated spot, so the type genuinely implies the invariant
TypeScript only allows one cast per type
Casting elsewhere is a runtime error
The compiler tracks how many casts a program contains
quiz.explanation: The brand is only as trustworthy as the assertions that create it. Scattering casts around means the type no longer proves anything.

quiz.question: How can you check at runtime whether a value is a `UserId`?
options: You cannot directly — you must re-run the validation the constructor performs
quiz.explanation: Since the brand is erased there is nothing to inspect. Runtime questions about a branded value always come back to re-checking the underlying data.

flashcards.front: How should branded values be created?

flashcards.front: What does `readonly` on a property prevent?

flashcards.front: `readonly number[]` vs `ReadonlyArray<number>`?

flashcards.front: What does `Object.freeze` do that `readonly` doesn't?

flashcards.front: What is aliasing, and why is it a bug source?

quiz.question: When is a generic the WRONG tool?
options: When the body never uses T — a plain parameter type is clearer
When there is more than one type parameter
quiz.explanation: A type parameter used once and never related to anything else adds noise without adding a guarantee.

quiz.question: `function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined` — what does `first([1, 2])` return, type-wise?
quiz.explanation: `T` is inferred as `number`; the `| undefined` covers the empty array.

quiz.question: `function len<T extends { length: number }>(x: T) { … }` — what is `len(5)`?
quiz.explanation: The constraint rejects arguments without a numeric `length`.

quiz.question: `class Box<T> { value: T; constructor(v: T) { this.value = v; } }` — what is `new Box(3).value`'s type?
quiz.explanation: `T` is inferred from the constructor argument and widened to `number` for the mutable field.

quiz.question: `first<string>([1])` — result?
quiz.explanation: An explicit type argument fixes `T`, and the argument must match it.

quiz.question: What does `function merge<A, B>(a: A, b: B): A & B` promise?
options: A value with every property of both
quiz.explanation: `A & B` is an intersection: it has all members of both.

quiz.question: `get(user, "nme")` where `get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K)` — result?
options: Compile error: `"nme"` isn't a key of the user type
quiz.explanation: The `keyof` constraint turns a typo into an error at the call.

quiz.question: In `Promise<T>`, what is `T`?
options: The type of the value the promise resolves with
quiz.explanation: Rejections are untyped (`any`/`unknown`); only the fulfilment value is in the type.

quiz.question: You write a helper that only counts elements. Should it be `count<T>(xs: T[])` or `count(xs: unknown[])`?
options: `count(xs: unknown[])` — `T` would appear only once and link nothing
It makes no difference to callers, so either
quiz.explanation: A type parameter earns its place by connecting two positions (input and output). Otherwise `unknown` says the same thing more simply.

quiz.question: With `function f<const T extends readonly string[]>(xs: T)`, what is `T` for `f(["a", "b"])`?
quiz.explanation: A `const` type parameter (TS 5.0) infers as if the caller had written `as const`.

quiz.question: `function wrap<T>(x: T) { return [x]; }` — what is the inferred return type?
quiz.explanation: An array literal infers an array type, not a tuple, unless asked otherwise.

quiz.question: What does `NoInfer<T>` do in `function pick<T extends string>(options: T[], fallback: NoInfer<T>)`?
options: Makes `T` come from `options` only, so a `fallback` not in the list is an error
quiz.explanation: Without it, `pick(["a", "b"], "c")` would widen `T` to include `"c"` (TS 5.4).

quiz.question: When is a generic default like `<T = string>` used?
options: When `T` can be neither inferred nor is it passed explicitly
quiz.explanation: Inference and explicit arguments both take priority over the default.

quiz.question: Why is `function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T` better than `function longest(a: { length: number }, b: { length: number }): { length: number }`?
options: The generic returns the caller's exact type instead of collapsing it to { length: number }
The generic is faster at runtime
The non-generic version does not compile
quiz.explanation: Both accept the same arguments. The difference is on the way out: the generic hands back `string` for strings, while the plain signature loses everything except `.length`.

quiz.question: In `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, what is `T[K]`?
options: An indexed access type — the type of the property named K on T
An array of T indexed by K
quiz.explanation: `T[K]` looks up a property type by name, which is what lets one signature return `string` for `\"name\"` and `number` for `\"age\"`.

quiz.question: What does the default in `function makeBox<T = string>(value: T)` actually do?
options: It supplies T only when inference has nothing to infer from
It makes the value parameter optional
It coerces the argument to string
quiz.explanation: A type-parameter default is not a value default. `makeBox(1)` still infers `T = number`; the default matters for cases like `const b: Box = ...` where no argument drives inference.

flashcards.front: What problem do generics solve?
flashcards.back: Reusing code across types without losing precision: `first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined` returns a `number` for a `number[]`, not `any`.

flashcards.front: How are type arguments usually supplied?
flashcards.back: Inferred from the arguments: `first([1, 2])` infers `T = number`. Pass them explicitly only when inference can't see them.

flashcards.front: What does `<T extends { id: string }>` mean?

flashcards.front: What does `K extends keyof T` give you?
flashcards.back: A key that really exists on `T`, so `obj[key]` is typed `T[K]` — the value type for that exact key.

flashcards.front: Smell: a type parameter used only once. Why?
flashcards.back: It adds nothing — `<T>(x: T): void` is just `(x: unknown): void`. A generic earns its place by linking two positions.

flashcards.front: What is a generic default?
flashcards.back: `<T = string>` — the type used when `T` is neither passed nor inferable.

flashcards.front: Why might `T extends object` surprise you?
flashcards.back: Arrays and functions are objects too, so they satisfy it.

flashcards.front: What does TS2322 "'T' could be instantiated with an arbitrary type" mean?
flashcards.back: You returned a specific type where the caller chose `T`. The body must work for *every* `T`, not just the one you had in mind.

flashcards.front: What does a `const` type parameter do (TS 5.0)?
flashcards.back: `<const T>` infers literal types for arguments, as if the caller wrote `as const` — `f(["a", "b"])` infers `readonly ["a", "b"]`.

flashcards.front: What is `NoInfer<T>` for (TS 5.4)?
flashcards.back: Blocking inference from one argument, so `T` is decided by the others — e.g. a default value that must match the options list.

flashcards.front: How do you type a generic `groupBy`?
flashcards.back: `function groupBy<T, K extends PropertyKey>(xs: T[], key: (x: T) => K): Map<K, T[]>`.

flashcards.front: Generic class — how is `T` fixed?
flashcards.back: At construction: `new Stack<number>()`, or inferred from constructor arguments.

weeks.title: Mapped Types
weeks.goal: Transform every property of a type at once — and build what the type describes.

problems.note: A container described by a derived type.

weeks.project: Reimplement `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick` and `Omit` from scratch in a `utils.d.ts`, then check each against the built-in with a type-level test.

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` produce?
options: Every property made required — the built-in Required<T>
A union of T's property types
quiz.explanation: The `-` prefix strips a modifier the source had. `-readonly` does the same for readonly.

quiz.question: What is `keyof (A | B)`?
options: The keys A and B have in COMMON
quiz.explanation: Only shared keys are safe to access on a value that might be either — a frequent surprise when mapping over a union.

quiz.question: `{ [K in "a" | "b"]: K }`?
quiz.explanation: Each key maps to its own literal.

quiz.question: Which built-in is `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`?
quiz.explanation: It adds `readonly` to every property.

quiz.question: Which built-in is `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`?
quiz.explanation: It adds `?` to every property.

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null }` describe?
options: `T` with every field also allowed to be `null`
quiz.explanation: A mapped type can transform each value type.

quiz.question: What happens when a homomorphic mapped type is applied to an array type?
options: It produces an array (or tuple) type, mapping the elements
It maps the array's method names
It produces an object with numeric keys
quiz.explanation: Mapped types over `keyof T` treat arrays and tuples specially, so `Partial<[number, string]>` is `[number?, string?]`.

quiz.question: What does the `-?` modifier do?
quiz.explanation: `-?` is how `Required<T>` is built.

quiz.question: What does `[K in keyof T as K extends `` `_${string}` `` ? never : K]` do?
options: Drops every key starting with an underscore
Adds an underscore to every key
quiz.explanation: Remapping a key to `never` removes it.

quiz.question: Is `Record<K, V>` itself a mapped type?
options: No, it's built in to the compiler
quiz.explanation: Most utility types are ordinary mapped or conditional types you could write yourself.

quiz.question: Which modifiers does a homomorphic mapped type (over `keyof T`) keep from `T`?
quiz.explanation: That's why `Partial<Readonly<T>>` is still read-only.

quiz.question: `keyof (A & B)`?
quiz.explanation: An intersection has every key of both. (`keyof (A | B)` is the reverse: only the shared keys.)

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T]: () => T[K] }` produce for `T = { a: number }`?
quiz.explanation: Each value type is wrapped in a function type.

quiz.question: Why does `DeepReadonly` need recursion?
options: `Readonly` only covers the top level; nested objects need the same treatment
quiz.explanation: `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }` walks every level.

quiz.question: In a mapped type's `as` clause, what happens to a key you map to `never`?
options: The property is removed from the result — this is how Omit works
quiz.explanation: Key remapping to `never` drops the entry entirely, which is exactly the mechanism behind filtering utilities like `Omit`.

quiz.question: You define `type Getters<T>` that renames keys to `getName`, `getAge`. What exists at runtime?
options: Nothing — you must still build the object yourself; the type only describes it
An object with those methods, generated by the compiler
A proxy that forwards property access
The original object with extra prototype methods
quiz.explanation: Mapped types are erased like every other type. They describe the shape your runtime code is obliged to produce, usually ending in a cast where the loop finishes.

flashcards.back: A type built by looping over keys: `{ [K in keyof T]: … }`.

flashcards.front: How do you remove `readonly` or `?` in a mapped type?

flashcards.front: How do you filter keys out in a mapped type?

flashcards.front: What is a homomorphic mapped type?

flashcards.front: How would you write `Record<K, V>` yourself?

flashcards.front: Why does `Readonly<T>` not protect nested objects?
flashcards.back: It maps one level only. A `DeepReadonly` recurses: `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }`.

flashcards.front: Why does `string & K` appear inside `Capitalize<…>` in a remap?
flashcards.back: `keyof T` may include `number` and `symbol`; `Capitalize` accepts only strings, so intersecting keeps the string keys.

flashcards.front: Do mapped types exist at runtime?
flashcards.back: No. If you need the object they describe, you build it yourself — the type only checks that you did.

flashcards.front: What does `{ [K in "a" | "b"]: number }` produce?
flashcards.back: `{ a: number; b: number }`.

quiz.question: `type NonNil<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T`. What is `NonNil<string | null>`?
quiz.explanation: T is naked, so the conditional distributes: `string` takes the else branch, `null` becomes `never`, and `never` vanishes from a union.

quiz.question: What is `IsString<any>` for `type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no"`?
quiz.explanation: `any` is assignable to everything and nothing simultaneously, so a conditional over it resolves to the union of both branches.

quiz.question: `type IsArr<T> = T extends unknown[] ? true : false;` — what is `IsArr<string[]>`?
quiz.explanation: `string[]` is assignable to `unknown[]`.

quiz.question: `type IsArr<T> = T extends unknown[] ? true : false;` — what is `IsArr<string[] | number>`?
quiz.explanation: A naked type parameter distributes over the union, checking each member separately.

quiz.question: `type Elem<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never;` — what is `Elem<number[]>`?
quiz.explanation: `infer E` captures the element type.

quiz.question: `type Elem<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never;` — what is `Elem<string>`?
quiz.explanation: `string` isn't an array, so the false branch runs.

quiz.question: `type First<T> = T extends [infer F, ...unknown[]] ? F : never;` — `First<[1, 2]>`?
quiz.explanation: `F` captures the first element of the tuple.

quiz.question: `type First<T> = T extends [infer F, ...unknown[]] ? F : never;` — what is `First<[]>`?
quiz.explanation: An empty tuple doesn't match `[infer F, ...unknown[]]`.

quiz.question: `type Args<T> = T extends (...a: infer A) => unknown ? A : never;` — `Args<(x: string) => void>`?
quiz.explanation: Rest-parameter position infers a tuple — this is how `Parameters` works.

quiz.question: `Exclude<string | number | boolean, number>`?
quiz.explanation: Members assignable to `number` are removed.

quiz.question: `[never] extends [never] ? 1 : 2`?
quiz.explanation: Wrapped in a tuple there's no distribution, and `[never]` is assignable to itself.

quiz.question: `type T = any extends string ? 1 : 2`?
quiz.explanation: `any` as the checked type takes both branches.

quiz.question: Where may `infer` appear?
options: Only in the `extends` clause of a conditional type
quiz.explanation: It declares a variable for the pattern being matched.

quiz.question: `type Unbox<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? Unbox<V> : T;` — `Unbox<Promise<Promise<1>>>`?
quiz.explanation: The recursion peels one promise per step until none are left.

quiz.question: What does `infer` do inside a conditional type?
options: Binds a fresh type variable to whatever type matched at that position
Forces TypeScript to re-infer the whole expression
Declares a default for the type parameter
Converts a value into a type
quiz.explanation: `T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T` matches T against 'array of something' and names that something `U` — pattern matching on the type's structure.

quiz.question: How do you stop a conditional type from distributing over a union?
options: Wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [U] ? X : Y
Use an interface instead of a type alias
quiz.explanation: Distribution requires a bare type parameter on the left. Putting it inside a tuple makes it non-naked, so the check runs once against the whole union.

flashcards.front: Why does a function returning a conditional type usually need a cast inside?

weeks.title: Template Literals & Recursive Types
weeks.goal: Encode naming conventions in the type system, and describe unbounded data.

problems.note: A recursive structure with a recursive type.

weeks.project: Write an `events.ts` where the entity and action lists are `as const` arrays, the event-name type is a template literal over them, and a typed emitter rejects any name not in the catalogue.

quiz.question: Where can `Capitalize<T>` be used?
options: Only inside template literal types — it is a compiler intrinsic
quiz.explanation: `Capitalize`, `Uppercase`, `Lowercase` and `Uncapitalize` live purely in the type system. Capitalizing a real string is still your own code.

quiz.question: Why is `type Bad = Bad | string` an error while `type Json = string | Json[]` is fine?
options: A recursive alias must go through an object, array or function
type aliases cannot be recursive at all
quiz.explanation: `Bad` refers to itself with nothing to defer into. Wrapping the recursion in `Json[]` gives the checker a structure to expand lazily.

quiz.question: What does `T extends readonly [unknown, ...infer Rest]` accomplish?
options: Peels the first tuple element and binds the rest, enabling recursion
Checks T is a readonly array
quiz.explanation: It is the type-level head/tail destructure — the shrinking step every recursive tuple algorithm needs.

quiz.question: Which string does `` `id-${number}` `` accept?
quiz.explanation: `${number}` matches anything that parses as a number, fractions included.

quiz.question: `Uppercase<"ab">`?
quiz.explanation: The intrinsic string types transform literal types.

quiz.question: `` type H<S> = S extends `${infer X}${infer R}` ? X : never; `` — what is `H<"abc">`?
quiz.explanation: An `infer` followed by another placeholder captures a single character.

quiz.question: `` type Trim<S> = S extends ` ${infer R}` ? Trim<R> : S; `` — `Trim<"  x">`?
quiz.explanation: Each recursive step removes one leading space.

quiz.question: What does `` `${string}` `` match?
quiz.explanation: It's equivalent to `string` on its own; it's useful as part of a larger pattern.

quiz.question: Which is a valid recursive type for a tree?
quiz.explanation: The recursion sits inside an object type, so it's deferred and well-founded.

quiz.question: `` `${Uppercase<"get">}_${"a" | "b"}` ``?
quiz.explanation: Only the first part is uppercased; the union distributes over the second.

quiz.question: `Capitalize<"hello world">`?
quiz.explanation: Only the very first character is changed.

quiz.question: What does `` "42" extends `${infer N extends number}` ? N : never `` give (TS 4.8+)?
quiz.explanation: An `infer … extends number` constraint in a template parses the matched text into a number literal.

quiz.question: Why is `type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json }` allowed?
options: The self-references sit inside array and object types, so they're resolved lazily
Because it has a base case
quiz.explanation: A bare `type Bad = Bad | string` has nothing to defer and is rejected.

quiz.question: How many members does `` type T = `${"a" | "b"}-${"x" | "y" | "z"}` `` have?
quiz.explanation: Interpolating unions produces the cross product — 2 × 3 = 6 literal types. This growth is also why deeply nested templates can blow the compiler's limits.

quiz.question: Why does `function toSize(v: number, u: Unit): Size { return `${v}${u}` as Size; }` need the cast?
options: A template built from a runtime `number` widens to `string`, which the compiler cannot prove matches the pattern
Casts are always required when returning template literals
Unit is a union, and unions cannot be interpolated
quiz.explanation: Type-level interpolation over `${number}` works on literal types. A runtime value produces an ordinary `string`, so you assert the invariant your code maintains.

quiz.question: In `type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[K]> : T[K] }`, what is the base case?
options: A property whose type is not an object, which stops the recursion
quiz.explanation: The conditional decides at each property whether to recurse. Primitives take the else branch and terminate that path.

practice.prompt: Implement `Params<Path>`: the union of `:name` segments in a route like `"/users/:id/posts/:postId"`.
practice.hint: Two cases: a parameter followed by more path, and a parameter at the very end.
hints: Two cases: a parameter followed by more path, and a parameter at the very end.
Collect each captured name into a union, recursing on the rest.
practice.starter:
type Params<Path extends string> =
  ____;
practice.solution:
type Params<Path extends string> =
  Path extends `${string}:${infer P}/${infer Rest}` ? P | Params<Rest>
  : Path extends `${string}:${infer P}` ? P
  : never;

practice.title: Reverse a tuple
practice.prompt: Implement `Reverse<T>`.
practice.hint: Peel off the head, reverse the rest, put the head at the end.
hints: Peel off the head, reverse the rest, put the head at the end.
`[...Reverse<R>, H]`.
practice.starter: type Reverse<T extends unknown[]> = ____;
practice.solution: type Reverse<T extends unknown[]> = T extends [infer H, ...infer R] ? [...Reverse<R>, H] : [];

practice.title: The length of a tuple
practice.prompt: Implement `Length<T>` for a tuple: its length as a number literal.
practice.hint: A tuple's `length` property has a literal type.
hints: A tuple's `length` property has a literal type.
`T["length"]`.
practice.starter: type Length<T extends readonly unknown[]> = ____;
practice.solution: type Length<T extends readonly unknown[]> = T["length"];

practice.title: snake_case to camelCase
practice.prompt: Implement `Camel<S>`: `"foo_bar_baz"` becomes `"fooBarBaz"`.
practice.hint: Split at the first underscore.
hints: Split at the first underscore.
Capitalize the camel-cased tail and glue it to the head.
practice.starter: type Camel<S extends string> = ____;
practice.solution: type Camel<S extends string> = S extends `${infer Head}_${infer Tail}` ? `${Head}${Capitalize<Camel<Tail>>}` : S;

practice.title: A type for any JSON value
practice.prompt: Define `Json` so that any value `JSON.parse` could return is assignable to it — and a function is not.
practice.hint: Four primitive cases, then arrays and objects of JSON.
hints: Four primitive cases, then arrays and objects of JSON.
The type refers to itself inside `Json[]` and the object type.
practice.starter: type Json = ____;
practice.solution: type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [key: string]: Json };

weeks.title: Classes & Encapsulation
weeks.goal: Use classes where they pay — real privacy, invariants and accessors.

problems.note: Two structures kept in step behind one interface.

weeks.project: Write an `account.ts` with a `BankAccount` class whose balance is `#private`, exposing `deposit`, `withdraw` (rejecting overdrafts) and a computed `balance` getter.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `#count` and `private count`?
options: `#` is enforced by the JavaScript engine; `private` is erased at compile time
`#` cannot be used in generic classes
quiz.explanation: A `private` field is visible to any JavaScript that ignores the types. A `#` field is genuinely inaccessible from outside the class.

quiz.question: Why do arrow-function class fields fix the `this` problem?
options: They capture `this` from the instance at construction rather than at call time
They are bound by the compiler
They cannot be detached from the object
quiz.explanation: Passing `obj.method` as a callback loses the receiver. An arrow field closes over `this` when the instance is built, so it travels with the function.

quiz.question: What does a `get` accessor let you do?
options: Expose a computed value through property syntax
quiz.explanation: Getters compute on access; `set` accessors are the ones that validate assignment. `readonly` is a separate modifier.

quiz.question: When should you NOT reach for a class?
options: When the thing is plain data with no invariant to protect
When there is more than one instance
quiz.explanation: Data with no behaviour is better as a plain object plus functions — it stays serializable and structurally typed.

quiz.question: Why does `const f = obj.method; f();` often break?
options: `this` is lost when the method is detached from its receiver
Methods cannot be assigned to variables
It only breaks in strict mode
quiz.explanation: A plain method call binds `this` from the call site. An arrow-function class field, or an explicit bind, keeps the receiver attached.

quiz.question: What does `readonly` on a class field prevent?
options: Mutating the object the field points at
quiz.explanation: It is a compile-time restriction on reassigning the field. The object it references can still be mutated freely.

quiz.question: `class A { #x = 1; static read(a: A) { return a.#x; } }` — allowed?
options: Yes — code inside the class can read `#x` on any `A`
quiz.explanation: Private names are scoped to the class body, not to one instance.

quiz.question: `class A { private x = 1 }` — `new A().x` from outside?
options: Compile error, but at runtime the property is there
quiz.explanation: `private` is checked by the compiler only. `#x` is the runtime-private version.

quiz.question: In a subclass constructor, `this.y = 1; super();` — result?
options: Error: `super()` must be called before `this` is used
quiz.explanation: The object doesn't exist until the parent constructor has run (TS17009).

quiz.question: Where do `static` members live?
options: On the class itself, not on instances
quiz.explanation: Access them as `ClassName.member`.

quiz.question: Can a `readonly` class field be assigned in the constructor?
options: Yes — only after construction is it fixed
quiz.explanation: `readonly` fields may be set at the declaration or in the constructor.

quiz.question: Does `implements I` give a class any code from `I`?
options: No — an interface has no implementation; it only checks
quiz.explanation: `implements` is a check. Inheritance of code comes from `extends`.

quiz.question: Assigning to a property that has a `get` but no `set`?
quiz.explanation: A getter without a setter is typed `readonly` (TS2540).

quiz.question: In a `static` method, what does `this` refer to?
quiz.explanation: That's why `this.create()` works inside a static factory.

quiz.question: `({ x: 1, y: 2 }) instanceof Point` for a class `Point { x = 0; y = 0 }`?
quiz.explanation: `instanceof` checks the prototype chain, not the shape. Structural typing is compile-time only.

quiz.question: Which is composition rather than inheritance?
quiz.explanation: The car *has* an engine instead of *being* one — swap it without touching a hierarchy.

exam.title: Bank account with invariants
exam.prompt: Write a `BankAccount` class with a `#balance`, a `deposit`, a `withdraw` that refuses overdrafts, and a `balance` getter. The input is `n` then `n` commands (`deposit n`, `withdraw n`). Print the balance after each command, printing `refused` instead when a withdrawal would overdraw, then the final balance.
exam.hint: The invariant lives inside the class: withdraw is the only path that reduces #balance, and it refuses rather than going negative.

flashcards.front: `private` vs `#private`?
flashcards.back: `private` is compile-time only — the field is a normal property at runtime. `#field` is truly private, enforced by JavaScript.

flashcards.front: What is a class invariant?
flashcards.back: A rule that holds after every public method, e.g. "balance is never negative". Private state plus checked methods enforce it.

flashcards.front: What does `implements` check?
flashcards.back: That the class has every member of the interface. It does not inherit anything or change the class's type.

flashcards.front: When does `protected` make sense?
flashcards.back: When a subclass needs access but outside code shouldn't — it means nothing without a subclass.

flashcards.front: What does `override` guard against?
flashcards.back: Typos and base-class renames: with `noImplicitOverride`, a method that doesn't really override anything is an error.

flashcards.front: Can you instantiate an `abstract` class?
flashcards.back: No (TS2511). It exists to be extended; `abstract` methods have to be implemented by subclasses.

flashcards.front: Why can a detached method crash?
flashcards.back: `const f = obj.method; f()` calls it with `this` undefined. Bind it, wrap it in an arrow, or define it as an arrow field.

flashcards.front: Why are parameter properties (`constructor(private x: number)`) graded by type-check only here?
flashcards.back: They emit an assignment, so they aren't erasable — Node's strip-only mode refuses them.

flashcards.front: What does a getter give you over a plain field?
flashcards.back: A computed, read-only view: `get balance() { return this.#balance; }` — callers can read, not write.

flashcards.front: Classes are structural too — what does that mean?
flashcards.back: An object literal with the same public members is assignable to the class type; `instanceof` is the check that really needs the class.

flashcards.front: When is a discriminated union better than a class hierarchy?
flashcards.back: When the set of variants is closed and you mostly *switch* on them — exhaustiveness checking beats virtual dispatch there.

flashcards.front: What is a static factory?
flashcards.back: `static from(raw: string): Account | null` — a named constructor that can validate and fail, which `new` cannot.

weeks.title: Iterators, Generators & Generic Data Structures
weeks.goal: Produce values lazily and build containers that feel built-in.

problems.note: A container with an interface contract.

weeks.project: Write a `lazy.ts` with generator-based `range`, `map`, `filter`, `take` and `chunk`, then use them to process an infinite sequence without materialising it.

quiz.question: What does `yield*` do?
options: Delegates to another iterable, yielding all its values in place
Yields an array of the remaining values
quiz.explanation: It forwards every value from the inner iterable as if written inline — the standard way to compose generators.

quiz.question: `function* g() { yield 1; yield 2; }` — `[...g()]`?
quiz.explanation: Spreading drains the generator.

quiz.question: `function* g() { yield 1; yield 2; }` — what does the third `next()` on one `g()` iterator return?
quiz.explanation: After the last `yield` the generator returns, and further calls report `done`.

quiz.question: Is a generator's `return` value visited by `for…of`?
quiz.explanation: `for…of` stops at `done: true` and ignores its `value`.

quiz.question: Stack vs queue order?
options: Stack is last-in first-out; queue is first-in first-out
Stack is FIFO; queue is LIFO
quiz.explanation: Stacks drive DFS and undo; queues drive BFS and scheduling.

quiz.question: Why use a ring buffer for a queue?
options: O(1) enqueue and dequeue without shifting elements
quiz.explanation: Head and tail indices wrap around a fixed array.

quiz.question: In an array-backed binary heap, where are the children of index `i`?
quiz.explanation: And the parent is `Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)`.

quiz.question: Cost of inserting at the head of a singly linked list?
quiz.explanation: Point the new node at the old head and update `head`.

quiz.question: What does iterating a `Map` with `for…of` yield?
quiz.explanation: Destructure them: `for (const [k, v] of map)`.

quiz.question: `Iterable<T>` vs `Iterator<T>`?
options: An iterable has `[Symbol.iterator]()`, which returns an iterator; an iterator has `next()`
An iterator has `[Symbol.iterator]`, an iterable has `next`
quiz.explanation: `for…of` asks the iterable for a fresh iterator, then calls `next()` until done.

quiz.question: Why a generic `Stack<T>` instead of a `Stack` that stores `any`?
options: So `pop()` returns `T | undefined` and callers keep their types
quiz.explanation: With `any`, every value that comes out has lost its type.

quiz.question: What happens the second time you iterate the SAME generator object?
options: Nothing is produced — a generator object is exhausted after one pass
It yields the values in reverse
quiz.explanation: The generator holds its own position. If callers may iterate more than once, hand back a function that creates a fresh generator each time.

quiz.question: Why does `take(naturals(), 4)` terminate even though `naturals()` never ends?
options: Generators are lazy — naturals only computes a value when take asks, and take stops asking
TypeScript detects the infinite loop and bounds it
naturals() is evaluated eagerly up to a default limit
The spread operator caps at 1000 elements
quiz.explanation: Laziness is the point: production is driven entirely by consumption. Spreading `naturals()` directly, with no `take`, really would hang.

quiz.question: Why should `pop()` be typed `T | undefined` rather than `T`?
options: An empty stack really does return undefined, and the type should say so
Generic methods cannot return a bare T
undefined is required for iteration to work
quiz.explanation: Typing it as `T` is a lie that hands the caller an `undefined` the compiler swears is a real value — precisely the class of bug the type system exists to prevent.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `#items` and `private items`?
options: `#items` is private at runtime too; `private` is erased and the field is visible in JavaScript
`#items` cannot be used in a generic class
quiz.explanation: `#` is a real JavaScript private field enforced by the engine. `private` is a compile-time-only marker, so anything ignoring the types can still reach the value.

quiz.question: Why does a generic `SortedList<T>` take a comparator instead of constraining `T extends Comparable`?
options: T is erased at runtime, so ordering must be supplied as a function the class can call
Comparable does not exist in the TypeScript standard library
Constraints cannot be used on classes
Comparators are faster than interface dispatch
quiz.explanation: Both parts are true — there is no built-in Comparable — but the underlying reason is erasure: nothing about `T` survives to run, so the behaviour has to be passed in as a value.

exam.title: Lazy pipeline over an infinite source
exam.prompt: Write generators `naturals`, `filter`, `map` and `take`. The input is `count divisor`. Take the first `count` naturals divisible by `divisor`, square them, and print them space-separated (or `(none)`), then their sum. Nothing infinite may be materialised.
exam.hint: take must `return` the moment it has enough — that is what stops the infinite source being pulled forever.

flashcards.front: What makes an object iterable?
flashcards.back: A `[Symbol.iterator]()` method returning an iterator — an object with `next()` returning `{ value, done }`.

flashcards.front: What is a generator?
flashcards.back: A `function*` that `yield`s values lazily; calling it returns an iterator that runs the body on demand.

flashcards.front: Why can a generator describe an infinite sequence safely?
flashcards.back: Nothing runs until a value is asked for — `take(naturals(), 5)` computes only five.

flashcards.front: What does `yield*` do?
flashcards.back: Delegates to another iterable, yielding each of its values in turn — handy for recursive tree traversal.

flashcards.front: Can a generator be iterated twice?
flashcards.back: No — it is a one-shot iterator. Call the generator function again for a fresh one.

flashcards.front: What is the `Generator<T, TReturn, TNext>` type?
flashcards.back: The yielded type, the final `return` type, and the type `next(value)` accepts.

flashcards.front: What hangs: spreading which kind of iterator?
flashcards.back: An infinite one — `[...naturals()]` never finishes.

flashcards.front: Why is `queue.shift()` a trap in BFS?
flashcards.back: `shift` is O(n) — it moves every remaining element. Use a head index into the array, or a ring buffer.

flashcards.front: How do you make a `LinkedList<T>` work with `for…of`?
flashcards.back: Give it `*[Symbol.iterator]() { for (let n = this.head; n; n = n.next) yield n.value; }`.

flashcards.front: What does a binary heap give you?
flashcards.back: O(log n) insert and remove-min, with O(1) peek — the engine of a priority queue.

flashcards.front: How does a generic priority queue know what "smaller" means?
flashcards.back: It takes a comparator, `(a: T, b: T) => number`, in its constructor.

flashcards.front: What are iterator helpers (ES2025)?
flashcards.back: `map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `toArray` directly on iterators — lazy pipelines without writing generators.

weeks.title: Errors & Async
weeks.goal: Make failure visible in the type, and run async work concurrently on purpose.

problems.note: Time-ordered state with clear failure modes.
Incremental computation you could plausibly make async.

weeks.project: Write a `fetchAll.ts` that loads several simulated resources concurrently, races each against a timeout, and returns a `Result` per resource — no exception escapes.

quiz.question: Under `strict`, what type does `catch (e)` give `e`?
quiz.explanation: Any value can be thrown, so TypeScript refuses to assume `Error`. Narrow with `instanceof` before reading properties.

quiz.question: `try { throw "oops"; } catch (e) { … }` — what is `e`?
options: The string `"oops"` — not an `Error`, and with no stack trace
quiz.explanation: Anything can be thrown. Throw `Error` objects so there's a message and a stack.

quiz.question: `async function f() { throw new Error("x"); }` — what does calling `f()` without `await` do?
options: Returns a rejected promise; nothing throws at the call site
quiz.explanation: An async function turns throws into rejections. Unawaited, the rejection goes unhandled.

quiz.question: What does this print? `console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4);`
quiz.explanation: Synchronous code first; then microtasks (promise callbacks); then timers.

quiz.question: What does `await 5` evaluate to?
quiz.explanation: Awaiting a non-promise wraps it in a resolved promise and gives the value back.

quiz.question: What does `Promise.all([])` do?
quiz.explanation: With nothing to wait for, it's already done.

quiz.question: What does `Promise.any` do when every promise rejects?
options: Rejects with an `AggregateError` holding all the reasons
quiz.explanation: It resolves on the first success; only total failure rejects.

quiz.question: Type of `await Promise.all([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve("a")])`?
quiz.explanation: `Promise.all` on a tuple keeps each position's type.

quiz.question: What happens to an unhandled promise rejection in modern Node?
quiz.explanation: Since Node 15 the default is to throw. Always `await` or `.catch`.

quiz.question: `function f() { try { return 1; } finally { console.log("f"); } }` — calling `f()`?
quiz.explanation: `finally` always runs, even after a `return`.

quiz.question: Why set `this.name = "ValidationError"` in a custom error class?
options: So logs and stack traces show which kind of error it is
quiz.explanation: The name prefixes the message in `String(err)` and in stacks.

quiz.question: After `if (e instanceof Error)`, what is `e` (from `catch (e)` under `strict`)?
quiz.explanation: `instanceof` narrows the `unknown` catch variable, so `e.message` is safe.

quiz.question: What makes `Result<T, E>` enforce error handling?
options: It is a discriminated union, so `value` is only reachable after checking `ok`
It throws if you ignore the error branch
E defaults to string, which cannot be ignored
quiz.explanation: The `ok` field is the discriminant. On the `false` branch there is no `value` property at all, so skipping the check is a type error rather than a runtime surprise.

quiz.question: When is throwing the better choice over returning a Result?
options: For bugs and unrecoverable invariant violations the caller cannot sensibly handle
quiz.explanation: Expected, recoverable failures belong in the return type. Genuinely exceptional situations — an impossible branch, a broken invariant — should unwind loudly.

quiz.question: What is the total time of `await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchOne))` versus awaiting inside a loop?
options: The maximum of the individual times, versus the sum of them
The same — Promise.all is just syntax
Depends on the number of CPU cores
quiz.explanation: `.map` starts every promise before `all` waits, so they overlap. Awaiting inside a loop starts each one only after the previous resolves.

quiz.question: How does `Promise.allSettled` differ from `Promise.all` on failure?
options: It never rejects; every entry becomes a fulfilled/rejected record you inspect
It rejects only if every promise fails
It resolves with the successful values and silently drops failures
quiz.explanation: `allSettled` always resolves with one `PromiseSettledResult` per input. That last behaviour — dropping failures — is what `Promise.any` approximates, and it is not what allSettled does.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `Promise.race` and `Promise.any`?
options: race settles with the first promise to settle either way; any waits for the first SUCCESS
any is the async version of race
quiz.explanation: `race` is the timeout pattern precisely because an early rejection wins. `any` ignores rejections until all of them fail, then rejects with an AggregateError.

exam.title: Concurrent loads with a Result
exam.prompt: `load(id)` resolves to `id * 10` after `id` ms but rejects for a negative id. Run every id concurrently, convert each outcome to a `Result`, and print `id=value` or `id=failed` in input order, then the number that succeeded and their total, space-separated.
exam.hint: allSettled never rejects, so one bad id cannot lose the others; converting each entry to a Result makes the caller handle both branches.

flashcards.front: What is the type of `e` in `catch (e)` under `strict`?
flashcards.back: `unknown` (`useUnknownInCatchVariables`). Narrow it — `e instanceof Error` — before reading `e.message`.

flashcards.front: Throw or return a `Result`?
flashcards.back: Return a `Result` for failures the caller is expected to handle (bad input); throw for bugs and truly exceptional states.

flashcards.front: What is `Error.cause` for?
flashcards.back: Chaining: `throw new Error("load failed", { cause: err })` keeps the original error attached.

flashcards.front: What does `finally` do if the `try` returns?
flashcards.back: It still runs — and a `return` inside `finally` overrides the `try`'s return, which is almost always a bug.

flashcards.front: What does `await` do?
flashcards.back: Pauses the async function until the promise settles, then resumes with its value — or throws its rejection.

flashcards.front: `Promise.all` vs `Promise.allSettled`?
flashcards.back: `all` rejects as soon as one promise rejects; `allSettled` waits for every one and reports each as fulfilled or rejected.

flashcards.front: `Promise.race` vs `Promise.any`?
flashcards.back: `race` settles with the first promise to settle, success or failure; `any` resolves with the first success, rejecting only if all fail.

flashcards.front: Why is `await` inside a `for` loop sometimes slow?
flashcards.back: It runs the operations one after another. Start them all and `await Promise.all(...)` to run them concurrently.

flashcards.front: What goes wrong with `items.forEach(async (x) => { await save(x); })`?
flashcards.back: `forEach` ignores the returned promises — nothing waits for the saves, and their errors go unhandled.

flashcards.front: What is `async function f(): Promise<number>`'s return type if the body returns `5`?
flashcards.back: `Promise<number>` — an async function always returns a promise.

flashcards.front: How do you keep async output deterministic?
flashcards.back: Collect the results and print them in input order — never let completion timing decide the output order.

flashcards.front: How do you add a timeout to a promise?
flashcards.back: Race it against a timer that rejects: `Promise.race([work, timeout(ms)])`, or pass `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` to an API that accepts a signal.

weeks.title: Modules, Declarations & Capstone
weeks.goal: Structure a real project, describe the code you do not own, and prove the six months.

problems.note: The hardest design problem in the bank — take your time.

weeks.project: Capstone: build a small typed CLI as a multi-file project — a `Result`-based parser, a branded id type, a generic store with an iterator, an ambient declaration for one host global, and `strict` plus `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` clean.

quiz.question: What does a `.d.ts` file emit at build time?
options: Nothing — it only describes types the runtime is assumed to provide
A module that must be imported
quiz.explanation: Declaration files are pure description. Declaring something the runtime lacks gives a ReferenceError with no compile-time warning.

quiz.question: Why must module augmentation use `interface` rather than `type`?
options: Interfaces merge across declarations; type aliases cannot be reopened
type is illegal inside declare module
Interfaces are erased and types are not
quiz.explanation: Declaration merging is interface-only, and it is what lets you ADD a field to a library type instead of shadowing it.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a default export and a named export?
options: A default can be imported under any name, which makes it easy to rename inconsistently
A default is faster to load
A module may have several defaults
quiz.explanation: Named exports keep one canonical spelling across the codebase, which is why many style guides prefer them for anything but a single obvious entry point.

quiz.question: What does `import type { X } from "./x"` guarantee?
options: The import is erased entirely, so no runtime module dependency is created
X must be a type alias, not an interface
The module is loaded but unused
quiz.explanation: It makes the type-only intent explicit, avoiding a runtime import that a bundler would otherwise have to keep — the point of `verbatimModuleSyntax`.

quiz.question: `export default function f() {}` — how can another file import it?
quiz.explanation: A default export has no fixed name at the import site.

quiz.question: What does `import * as m from "./m"` give you?
options: A namespace object holding every export
A copy of the file's source
quiz.explanation: Access them as `m.name`.

quiz.question: What does `export { a as b }` do?
options: Exports the local `a` under the public name `b`
quiz.explanation: Aliasing on export lets a module choose its public names.

quiz.question: `declare const x: number; console.log(x);` — with nothing else defining `x`, what happens at runtime?
quiz.explanation: `declare` only tells the compiler the value exists elsewhere. If it doesn't, the runtime disagrees.

quiz.question: How do you declare types for an untyped package `"lib"`?
quiz.explanation: An ambient module declaration describes the package's exports.

quiz.question: What does `verbatimModuleSyntax` require?
options: Type-only imports to be written with `import type`
All imports to use file extensions
quiz.explanation: Imports without `type` are kept in the output, so a type-only one must say so or the runtime would try to load it.

quiz.question: What does `esModuleInterop` mainly affect?
quiz.explanation: It lets `import fs from "fs"` work against a CommonJS module that has no real default export.

quiz.question: Which is a `.d.ts` declaration for a function `add`?
options: `export declare function add(a: number, b: number): number;`
`export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`
`export type add(a: number, b: number): number;`
quiz.explanation: Declarations have signatures and no bodies.

quiz.question: Why can circular imports bite at runtime?
options: One module may run before the other has finished initialising its exports
quiz.explanation: An import from a half-initialised module can be `undefined` (or in its temporal dead zone) when first used.

quiz.question: What does `isolatedModules` guarantee?
options: Each file can be transpiled on its own, without type information from other files
Each file runs in its own process
Every file has a default export
quiz.explanation: Single-file tools (esbuild, SWC, Node's stripping) need this: e.g. re-exporting a type must use `export type`.

quiz.question: What does `export type { User }` do at runtime?
quiz.explanation: Type-only exports and imports exist only for the compiler.

quiz.question: Why does a file using `declare global` usually need `export {};`?
options: It forces the file to be a module, which `declare global` requires
It prevents the globals from leaking
It is a convention with no effect
quiz.explanation: A file with no imports or exports is a script, and its top-level declarations are already global — so `declare global` is only meaningful (and only legal) inside a module.

exam.title: Capstone: typed record store
exam.prompt: Combine the programme: a branded `RecordId`, a `Result`-returning parser, a generic iterable `Store<T>`, and an ambient host global. The input is `n` then `n` lines of `id value` (ids must match `r-\\d+`). Print `added <id>` or `rejected <line>` per line, then the stored ids space-separated in insertion order, then the store size.
